abstract: Genetically encoded integrators, which convert transient signals into persistent optical signals, can provide unique insights into cell signaling, but the range of target species remains very limited. This work introduces the first photoactivatable integrator for L-lactate, Paint-Lac1, which operates through a ligand-modulated, irreversible {beta}-elimination reaction. Paint-Lac1 is composed of an LldR lactate binding domain fused to an mEos-derived photoconvertible protein. Upon irradiation with 405-nm light, Paint-Lac1 photoconverts to a stable bright orange state, and this process is inhibited by L-lactate. Mechanistic studies reveal that Paint-Lac1 has the same underlying photochemical mechanism as mEos-derived proteins yet exhibits a distinct photophysical outcome, driven by a chromophore environment that stabilizes the phenol form of the chromophore. A ratiometric variant, Paint-Lac1-EGFP, preserves the L-lactate-modulated integrator function and enables biosensor expression-independent quantification. We demonstrate that Paint-Lac1 can be used in mammalian cells to generate a persistent fluorescence signal that is inversely proportional to L-lactate concentration.
